lens: Clarity and depth for a curious 15-year-old and an expert at once. This film has no AlexNet or transformer sequence, so the lens's 'in-depth sequences' are read as the brief's three deep dives: ternary to relu, host loop and patterns, gradients through a program. One transformer link the bible does support (FR25, Q127) is proposed below.
runtimeCheck: node generator/film/script.mjs assemble --slug handwired-explained --check: errors 0, warnings 1, 'estimated 25.6 min (1538.1 s, at 140 wpm) against a 24.0 min target'; 2741 words, 182 lines, 103 shots. Inside the brief's 22-26 min range, so runtime is not critical. Headroom to the 26-minute ceiling is about 24 s. Every addition below must be paid for: trim the ch12-s07 credits hold from 21.6 s to 15 s (-6.6 s), and fold ch08-s06's silent 9 s into the line proposed for it. Re-run the check and stay at 25.9 min or under.
critical: ch06-s12 L0625 contradicts ch06-s05b L0615 in the same chapter. L0615 says one run per frame 'held until mid-September; now a busy drag frame runs about seventeen' (HL17). Ten lines later the narrator quotes the lab guide, 'One frame is one evaluation of a fixed-depth circuit', and endorses it ('Here it is'). An expert hears the film present a belief it has just retired as current. The quote is verbatim (Q127), but cut off this way it misleads. FIX, using another verbatim span of Q127 that also gives the film its one honest transformer link (FR25): 'The lab's guide compares it to a text-writing network, which adds one word and runs again: here, "the next-state write-back plays the role of the appended token". The host turns the crank. It never stops early.' Add FR25 to ch06-s12 claims. Change the OSD quote card to '"the appended token" — the lab guide' and keep 'an echo, not a citation' for the Kleene half only. FR25 shows the repo itself makes this comparison.

ch06-s03 L0608 misdescribes the spring step to the ear. 'One step multiplies two numbers, the window's distance from home and its speed' is heard as distance times speed. SP01 says one step is a 2x2 matrix applied to the pair (displacement, velocity). Because of this, L0609's 'four numbers' never gets defined either. FIX L0608: 'One step is a little grid of four numbers that mixes two others: the window's distance from home, and its speed. From rest, it comes out moving.' FIX L0609: 'Three hundred steps? Multiply that grid by itself, squared and squared again. JavaScript does it ahead; the program applies the four numbers that result, in fourteen operations, for any count.' (about +6 words; SP01, SP02)

issues.problem: The count trick doesn't add up by ear. The question is 'Which row is under the pointer?', and 'every row answers'. If every row answers that question, only one says yes, so 'count the yeses: three' sounds wrong. PT08: each row really answers 'is the pointer past my bottom edge?' (bottoms 40 80 80 140 180, pointer 90 give 1 1 1 0 0), and the count is the row's index.
issues.fix: 'A count. Which row is under the pointer? A loop stops at the first match. Here every row answers an easier question: is the pointer past my bottom edge? Count the yeses, three, and that's the row, counting from nought.' (+14 words.) OSD: add 'is pointer past my bottom?' above the bits.

issues.problem: Two threads are left hanging. (1) The finale names 'the README's claim to take "regular JavaScript"' as one of three still-argued beliefs, but the narration never voiced that claim. The README's first line (Q001, PJ01) appears only on screen. A teenager meets a contested belief for the first time in the last two minutes. (2) 'One guess falls at once, for the library itself' is a hedge the ear can't decode. Then in ch08 'the lab's compiler' arrives after the film has said no tool converts JS, which looks like a contradiction (LB09: a trace compiler for a defined numeric subset).
issues.fix: L0305: 'The README's first line does say "Turn your regular JavaScript code into a neural net". But the docs are plain: "No tool converts existing JavaScript source into a program." Its lab tried one, for a narrow subset; we'll come to that.' (about +25 words; add Q001/PJ01/PJ03/LB09 to ch03-s03 claims.) L1206 then pays off a belief the viewer has already met.

issues.problem: 'The longest chain of gates runs seventy-one deep' is a number with no consequence. Both audiences need to hear why it matters: CM07 says a layer-per-step backend can never run fewer steps than that chain. That is the hinge for ch05-s06 (the GPU was slower) and ch09 ('It is for many documents').
issues.fix: 'So at least seventy-one steps must wait their turn, one after another, on any machine: the longest chain of gates.' (+10 words; CM07.)

issues.problem: Partly fixed since round 2. 'Thirty-two-bit floats fall a hair short' still leaves out the column width, so nobody can check it by ear. It also doesn't say what the program does with the hair: floors it to six. Without that the lesson ('exact' means matching FP32, not doubles) has no punchline. EX03: f(f(1708) x f(1/244)) = 6.999999523162842, so columns >= 7 reads 0.
issues.fix: 'How many two-hundred-and-forty-four-pixel columns fit in a window seventeen hundred and thirty-two wide? Doubles say seven. Thirty-two-bit floats fall a hair short, so the window draws six, and the program matches the six exactly.' (+16 words.)

issues.problem: 'More precision broke it' is a lovely paradox, but nothing explains it, and 'went wrong' (L0427) never says wrong against what. EX10 together with EX07: labels pass through rounding points, where a last-digit difference turns into a different label. That is also the only reason the film gives that rounding points need FP32 order.
issues.fix: 'More precision broke the match: each label rounds, and a difference in the last digit, rounded, becomes a different label. Keep thirty-two-bit order at those rounding points alone, and every label came back.' (+12 words; add EX07, already in claims.)

issues.problem: Deep Dive I's best callback runs silent, carried by an OSD no teenager can parse in 9 s ('slope of 3·v at v = 0 → 0 · of v·3 → 3 | both ramps on their corners'). DG28 is the film's clearest proof that 'both branches and corners' matter for gradients too, and it appears only as small print.
issues.fix: Give it one line and pay for it with the plate's silent time: 'Even the slopes had a bug. Three times v, at nought, claimed no slope at all; v times three said three. Both ramps sat on their corners. Fixed that morning.' (about 28 words; minDuration 9 -> fit to the line.) Simplify OSD to '3·v at v = 0: slope 0 ✗ · v·3: slope 3 ✓'.

issues.problem: Deep Dive III never ties back to Deep Dive I. The valve's opening, 'g plus b, never below nought', IS the ramp from ch04 (PR02: reglu(left, gate) = left x max(0, gate)), but the narration doesn't say so. ch03-s05's 'a gated product' is likewise never explained as 'a ramp times a number'. An expert wonders where ReLU sits in the four-instruction set. A teenager misses that the one machine part has come back.
issues.fix: L0703: '...The opening is a ramp, like the lever's: g plus b, never below nought.' (+5 words.) Optionally L0309: '...a weighted sum, a ramp times a number, a snap to a whole number, a read from a list.'

issues.problem: The OSD '×2^14 · ×2^24 ×5 · ×2^15 = 2^149' reads as 2^14 x 2^24 x 5 x 2^15 = 5 x 2^53, which is false, so an expert pausing the frame sees a sum that doesn't work. The narration also hides why the magnification is staged at all: TE08 has six clamp stages plus a final scale.
issues.fix: OSD: '×2^14 · ×2^24 (five times) · ×2^15 = 2^149', with a small line under it: 'smallest float 2^−149 → 1'. L0420: '...It magnifies, in stages, by two to the hundred and forty-ninth.' (+2 words; TE08, EX05.)

issues.problem: 'the familiar loop' is never defined. Neither audience knows which loop is meant, so the 359 px drift is a number about nothing. HL18: the familiar render order is handle input, then new layout, then animation tick.
issues.fix: 'Replay one session at two frame rates. The usual order, input first, then animation, drifts up to three hundred and fifty-nine pixels apart.' (+3 words.)

issues.problem: 'Past three hundred steps in one frame' doesn't say when that would happen. A teenager can't picture a frame holding 300 steps. HL08: 300 steps is 1,200 ms of backlog.
issues.fix: 'If more than a second passes between frames, past three hundred steps, stepping stops and every window snaps home.' (+6 words.)

issues.problem: 'RegExp keeps up, and wins after a pause' is cryptic: it sounds as if RegExp pauses and then wins. JS13/JS19: after a 200 ms pause in typing, the GPU search takes 2-8x as long.
issues.fix: 'With eight workers, RegExp keeps up. And after a pause in typing, the GPU is slow to wake: RegExp wins, except on that one pattern.' (+8 words.)

issues.problem: Carried over: 'five design numbers' and 'to follow a drag' are still undefined. The dissent half of DG20 (24.6% of frames began with every slope at nought) is on screen only, so the ear hears a success with no caveat. That cuts against the film's own 'who doubted it' pattern.
issues.fix: 'The lab did unfreeze five hand-written numbers in one app's layout, and let a drag pull on them. One gradient step solved nearly two moving frames in three; in one in four, every slope began at nought.' (+10 words.)

issues.problem: 'which should change nothing' is still unexplained for the teenager, and 'error' was never introduced as a number that measures wrongness. LB04 names Adam's 1e-8 epsilon but not why scaling should be harmless. The bible doesn't support stating Adam's scale-invariance.
issues.fix: Bible-safe: 'Multiply its error score, the number learning shrinks, by a million: twenty out of twenty. A tiny safety constant in the learner, Adam, was swamping the slopes.' This drops the unexplained 'should change nothing'. If the historian adds a source for Adam's scale-invariance, restore it as 'which, for Adam, should change nothing'.

issues.problem: Carried over: 'Its parser is a table' assumes the viewer knows what a table-driven parser is, so 'valid input never reads most of it' has nothing to hang on.
issues.fix: 'Its parser is a table: for each state and each next character, what happens next. Valid input never reads most of it.' (+12 words; LB19, JS07.)

issues.problem: 'The search: eleven to fifteen' doesn't say this is the GPU (JS11). The next shot's GPU 4.5-5.2 ms (JS13, back to back) then looks like a contradiction. The OSD says 'back to back' only in s07.
issues.fix: L0912: '...The GPU search: eleven to fifteen.' (+1 word.) In the ch09-s06 OSD, label the 11-15 ms 'per keystroke' to match the s07 'back to back'.

issues.problem: 'The tree is slower here' leaves 'here' unclear. PT06: slower on the CPU executor; a GPU is where a tree can win. That was the ch05 lesson, and it is an easy callback.
issues.fix: 'The tree is slower on the main processor, but drifts far less.' (+2 words.)

issues.problem: 'add a huge odd number' comes right after 'past nearly seventeen million', so a listener can merge the two. The atom works at about 8.4 million (2^23 + 1), where floats are one apart. PR08.
issues.fix: '...add a huge odd number, about eight million, to a score, then take it away.' (+3 words.)

issues.problem: Quote integrity, low risk: the spoken variants turn numerals inside quotation marks into words ('32-bit' -> 'thirty-two-bit', '64' -> 'sixty-four', '11' -> 'eleven'). The check passes, but the brief forbids re-spelling quoted text in narration.
issues.fix: Keep the spoken quote spans identical to quotes.json and move the pronunciations into voice/lexicon (or confirm with the pipeline owner that numeral expansion is the sanctioned TTS path).

strengths: Deep Dive I is genuinely in depth and every number checks by hand. 4.5 gives bit 0.5 and 11. At 16,777,222 the second ramp's input 16,777,217 ties to the even 16,777,216, so the bit is 2 and the answer 8. 8,388,609.5 ties to 8,388,610, giving 1. The grid compare relu(1 - relu(5 - a)) is two operations against the sign cascade's sixteen. The ramp / bit / shutter build gives a teenager a machine and an expert the exact formulas on screen.

The tag device answers the lens's era question on almost every belief: who tied it on, who doubted it, how long it held. Logic gate: McCulloch and Pitts 1943, Gidon 2020, frayed as biology and held as engineering. Learn-don't-write: Sutton, then Brooks six days later. Compiling is a dead end: unnamed July briefs, the September reassessment, about eight weeks. GPU is faster: hours. Each one is said aloud, not just shown.

Most round-2 clarity fixes landed: 'about seven digits' for FP32 (L0310), the infinity hypothetical (L0408), the twenty-thousand-labels rewrite (L0427), running totals named (L0617), the save/replay/discard frame (L0614), seventeen evaluations (L0615), the checker's early-return bug (L0808), XOR on screen (L0208b), the DSL gloss (L1001), the input three (L0703) and the 'three beliefs' count (L1206).

Deep Dive III works a ReGLU forward and backward with real numbers (0.15, 0.225, 0.45, 1.5; correct per PR02), defines 'slope, or gradient' before it uses it, and makes the closed-gate death and its weight-decay cure concrete. It then says plainly that the gallery is a small generic network, not an unfrozen program (DG06): honest limits, stated aloud.

Even-handed throughout: Sutton/Brooks, the HN commenters on both sides, the Claude Code and Codex disclosure with 'This film was written with Claude', the TOML failure judged by a rule fixed beforehand, and 'not delivered by these experiments'. The film models how a belief should end.
